questions_and_answers.question: In sentences with both a direct and indirect object, which comes first?
What is notable about object order in German sentences beginning with the verb?

answers.answer: A pronoun object may precede a noun subject
The noun subject must precede everything
Objects are always at the end

questions_and_answers.question: In the example 'Nehmen Sie täglich dreimal je fünfzehn Tropfen ...', what is being prescribed?

answers.answer: Fifteen drops of medicine three times a day

questions_and_answers.question: What happens when both objects are pronouns?

answers.answer: The accusative pronoun precedes the dative pronoun
The dative pronoun precedes the accusative pronoun
The pronouns appear at the end

questions_and_answers.question: Which sentence shows a pronoun object preceding a noun object?

answers.answer: Ich habe es dem Arzt gesagt
Der Arzt hat es mir gesagt
Herr Becker diktierte seiner Sekretärin einen langen Brief
Dr. Buchner hat meiner Frau eine Kur verordnet

questions_and_answers.question: What is the English meaning of 'Blieb Ihnen noch Zeit für private Interessen?'

answers.answer: Did you have any time left for your private interests?
Do you still have interest in work?
Are you interested in private matters?

questions_and_answers.question: Which example illustrates two noun objects in a dative-accusative order?

answers.answer: Herr Becker diktierte seiner Sekretärin einen langen Brief
Ich habe sie dem nicht gezeigt
Er hat Ihnen das schon gebracht

questions_and_answers.question: In 'Wieviel kostet der Anzug? Gut, packen Sie ihn mir bitte ein.' what is being requested?
Why is object order important in German?

answers.answer: It clarifies relationships between pronouns and nouns
It determines the gender of nouns

questions_and_answers.question: Which pronoun placement is correct when both objects follow the verb?

articles.text:
WORD ORDER - NOUNS AND PRONOUNS
Up to now in talking about word order we have been mainly concerned with the position of the finite, or inflected verb in the sentence. Let us now examine the place of noun and pronoun objects in the following sentences, most of which have occurred in the preceding units:
Nehmen Sie täglich dreimal je fünfzehn Tropfen von der Medizin, für die ich Ihnen jetzt ein Rezept gebe. (Take fifteen drops three times a day of something I'll give you a prescription for.)
Konnten Sie ihm nicht noch schnell ein paar Zeitungen holen, ehe der Zug abfuhr? (Couldn't you still hurry and get him a couple of newspapers before the train left?)
Empfehlen Sie mich bitte Ihrer Frau Gemahlin. (Please remember me to Mrs....)
Mein achtjähriger Sohn hat sich das Knie aufgeschlagen. (My eight-year-old son [fell and] scraped his knee.)
Ich habe es dem Arzt gesagt. (I said it to the doctor.)
In sentences in which a direct and indirect object (or an object and an interested bystander) occur, you will notice that the PRONOUN OBJECT consistently PRECEDES the NOUN OBJECT with its specifier and modifiers.
Now note the following examples:
Wenn Sie den Jungen jetzt gleich bringen würden, könnte ihn Herr Doktor sofort behandeln. (If you'd bring the boy right to the office now the doctor could treat him immediately.)
Blieb Ihnen noch Zeit für private Interessen? (Did you have any time left for [your own] private interests?)
Deshalb interessierte mich der Wiederaufbau. (That's why the reconstruction interested me.)
Übrigens wollte Sie ein Herr von der englischen Botschaft sprechen. (By the way a gentleman from the British Embassy wanted to talk to you.)
Here it can be seen that a PRONOUN OBJECT may precede a NOUN SUBJECT with its specifier and modifiers in sentences beginning with the verb or with another word than the subject.
Now also note these examples:
Wieviel kostet der Anzug? Gut, packen Sie ihn mir bitte ein. (How much does the suit cost? All right; wrap it up for me please.)
Ich glaube, Fräulein Bruce hat eine Schreibmaschine. Sie leiht sie Ihnen sicher gern. (I think Miss Bruce has one. I'm sure she'll be glad to lend it to you.)
When both objects of a verb are pronouns the ACCUSATIVE PRONOUN usually PRECEDES THE DATIVE PRONOUN. Note that pointing words, however, generally follow other pronouns when both objects follow the verb.
Er hat Ihnen das schon gestern gebracht. (He brought you that yesterday already.)
Ich habe sie dem nicht gezeigt. (I didn't show them to him.)
Here are a few sentences in which both objects of the verb are nouns:
Herr Becker diktierte seiner Sekretärin einen langen Brief. (Mr. Becker dictated a long letter to his secretary.)
Dr. Buchner hat meiner Frau eine Kur in Bad Nauheim verordnet. (Dr. Buchner prescribed treatment at Bad Nauheim for my wife.)
In sentences of this type DATIVE NOUN OBJECTS PRECEDE ACCUSATIVE NOUN OBJECTS with their specifiers and modifiers.
